models.best: Inferred from its principle that work is pooled through reciprocal obligation, so help comes back when a household is short-handed and trust, not a wage contract, keeps labour shared. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that gifts create obligations to return, so refusing to repay labour can cost standing and alliances, while hours and rest follow what kin and allies expect rather than any fixed limit or leave. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift; Sahlins, Stone Age Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a family farm balances the work its members can do against the household's needs, so hours rise and fall with need rather than with a price for labour. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves consumption, so when a household's needs outrun its labour, members work longer hours in peak seasons with no outside limit on hours and no wage or statutory leave to rebalance the work. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central authority stores collected goods and redistributes them to workers and officials, so workers can be supplied in lean seasons and labour for central works can be planned in advance. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that goods are collected as tribute or taxes, so labour can be owed to the centre as a levy, with hours and rest set by officials and no right for workers to leave. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation; Polanyi, Arensberg and Pearson, Trade and Market in the Early Empires

models.best: Inferred from its principle that output is sold through trade, so in the model's own terms hours are set in one place by the owner around the crop and the sale of output, giving a single planned calendar. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through the ownership of people, so hours, rest and leave have no legal limit, and the enslaved are denied the education and property with which they could bargain over any of them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that peasants owe labour services and rents in return for land, protection and justice, so each obligation is fixed in advance and known to both lord and peasant. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the manor is largely self-supplying, so a peasant's time is partly owed to the lord as labour services, with no statutory limit on hours and no leave that the peasant can claim as of right. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society; Capitulare de villis

models.best: Inferred from its principle that statutes govern entry and training, so apprentices and journeymen work under written rules that set how each stage of training is completed. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that masters control entry and set the statutes, so newcomers wait for places, journeymen have little say over hours or terms, and the rules are written by those who gain from them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Boileau, Le Livre des métiers; Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates production and trade for a surplus, so hours and conditions in favoured trades can be set by statute for national ends. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour and output serve a trade surplus, so hours and effort are set for export output rather than for workers' rest or leave, and workers in regulated trades have no say in the rules that bind them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade; Heckscher, Mercantilism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a single tax on the rent of land funds the state and leaves wages and labour untaxed, so a worker keeps the full return on the hours worked. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture makes a net product, so labour in manufacture and services is treated as yielding no net gain, and the hours and rest of such workers receive little protection in the scheme. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Quesnay, Tableau économique; Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: Kellogg's six-hour day at Battle Creek shows a plant splitting its workday into four six-hour shifts from 1930, a work-sharing response to the Depression, which accounts tie to higher productivity, lower labour costs and fewer accidents. Job counts and pay figures conflict between accounts and are unconfirmed.
models.worst: Where hours are left to private contract, no legal cap protects workers, and manufacturers and free-trade Liberals resisted state limits on hours on laissez-faire grounds. Britain's Ten Hours Act for textile mills capped the working day at ten hours for women and young people, after years of pressure from campaigners. Its terms come from encyclopaedia summaries, not the Act's text, and sources disagree on who was covered. Source: Online encyclopaedia (secondary), entries on the Factories Act 1847 and on the Ten Hours Act; Mount Royal Undergraduate Humanities Review (student journal, year not shown in the results)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, so hours and leave are best matched to local conditions by the employers and workers who face them rather than by a central plan. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit expansion and state planning distort production, so a credit-fuelled boom can bring long hours and overtime, followed by a bust in which layoffs end them abruptly. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Menger, Grundsätze der Volkswirthschaftslehre; Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that deregulation and fewer controls on markets let employers and workers agree hours and leave directly, so working time adjusts to demand and to what each worker prefers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The EU Working Time Directive and the UK opt-out shows where deregulation can let individual consent displace a legal cap: the 1993 Directive set a 48-hour average weekly ceiling, and UK rules let a worker's written consent displace it. Unions said about a third of signatories had no genuine option, but these are one side's estimates, and estimates of the share of workers above 48 hours differ. Source: Trades Union Congress (TUC), report and a late-2008 document; Cambridge academic research project; Pinsent Masons (law-firm news on the 2004 consultation); a company blog on the Commission's review (year not shown in the results)

models.best: Keynesian welfare capitalism can use state working-time policy to keep employment high: France's 35-hour week and the 2002 assessment put the job effect at roughly 300,000 positions, as Eurofound relayed the government's own estimate, and no independent estimate is given here.
models.worst: Kellogg's six-hour day at Battle Creek shows that work-sharing in a slump can cut weekly pay: a 1932 Labor Department payroll review concluded that 77 percent of workers earned less each week. That review is known only through accounts, and job counts and pay figures conflict between them and are unconfirmed. Source: InformationWeek (technology trade publication, article; year not shown in the results); other accounts in the results are blogs and podcast pages

models.best: The EU Working Time Directive and the UK opt-out shows a legal order with worker voice: the 1993 Directive sets a 48-hour average weekly ceiling, averaged over reference periods of up to four months that collective agreement can extend. Its sources are mostly union, law-firm and company pages, so the detail is contested.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that worker representation in firms depends on bargaining strength, so where unions are weak, hours and leave are set mainly on employers' terms, and a legal order that curbs monopoly does not by itself secure working time. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft; Erhard, Wohlstand für Alle

models.best: Sweden's parental insurance and fathers' take-up: a digest dates the first reserved-month quota in Swedish parental leave to 1995, and a 2005 working paper reports around 85% of fathers used some leave. Causation is speculative.
models.worst: Sweden's parental insurance and fathers' take-up: most spells were short, and men's share of claimed parental days has levelled off at about 31% since 2018, though other sources put it at roughly a third. That share comes from a policy brief drawing on Statistics Sweden data, official agency statistics are not cited here, and causation is speculative. Source: Population Europe (digest, year not shown in the results); Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research (working paper, 2005); Free Policy Briefs (policy brief, 2024, citing Statistics Sweden data)

models.best: South Korea's 52-hour weekly ceiling: when the rule took hold in July 2018, the weekly ceiling fell from 68 to 52 hours and the allowance for extra hours beyond the 40-hour base fell from 28 to 12, and annual hours fell by about 10% over a decade from a 2011 peak. The start date is disputed, and the figures are news coverage of OECD data.
models.worst: South Korea's 52-hour weekly ceiling sits alongside hours that remained high: Korea ranked fifth of 38 OECD members in 2021 at 1,915 hours against an OECD average of 1,716. The pandemic also trimmed hours, and the entry of Colombia and Costa Rica into the OECD accounts for much of the lower ranking, so the rule's effect cannot be isolated. Source: Asia News Network (news article, year not shown in the results); journal abstract (journal name and year not shown in the results); online encyclopaedia (secondary), for the disputed start date

models.best: Inferred from its principle that land value is taxed rather than labour and capital, so labour and capital are left untaxed and workers keep more of what their hours earn. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land value left untaxed fuels speculation and rent, so workers may need longer hours to pay for land, and a tax on land alone sets no limit on hours or leave. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities and planned associations replace wage competition, so hours and rest are arranged by the members who live and labour together and work is shared among them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities are built by example rather than by law, so hours and leave depend on each community's own goodwill and hold only while members keep to the plan, with no guaranteed limit or leave for members who leave. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Owen, A New View of Society; Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit and free contracts let workers keep the full value of their work, with banks lending at cost, so hours and leave are agreed by the workers who produce and keep the return. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free contracts govern work, so a worker who needs credit or has little bargaining power accepts the hours and leave on offer, and mutual credit spreads risk only among those inside the network. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control firms, one member one vote, and share the surplus between users and workers, so working time and leave are set by the members who do the work. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that members vote as owners, so a majority can set long hours or cut leave for a minority, and workers in the firm who are not members have no vote on their own hours. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers; Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods are shared by need within federated communes and that free association replaces contracts, so work is given as needed and hours are not set by any wage bargain. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there are no wages and no state, so no body can set or enforce hours, rest or leave, and workers depend on the commune's consensus, which can be slow and uneven in its outcomes. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Inferred from its principle that trade unions run industry through workers' organisations, so hours and leave are set by the workers who do the work, using strikes when needed. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that industry is run through strikes and eventually a general strike, so a dispute over hours can halt whole sectors and leave the wider public without a settled working-time rule. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the French CGT; Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail

models.best: Britain's Ten Hours Act for textile mills shows democratic, gradual reform at work: after years of pressure from campaigners, Parliament capped the working day at ten hours for women and young people. Its terms come from encyclopaedia summaries, not the Act's text.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that change comes by democratic and gradual stages, so hours and leave limits may arrive late and remain partial until later measures are passed. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fabian Essays in Socialism; Founding of the Fabian Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control of industry through guild-like councils, so each trade's hours and leave are set by those who work in it, with the state as one partner among several. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that control is split among several partners, so hours and leave can stall between councils and the state, and a trade's decisions may not reach workers outside it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry

models.best: Under the Soviet continuous production week, output rose in 1929 and 1930, the scheme's first two years. The start date is disputed, and the sources are popular history, commentary and a blog, so the figures are unconfirmed.
models.worst: Soviet continuous production week: officials ended up conceding more idle equipment despite output gains, the five-day cycle had shifted to six days by 1931, and the scheme was dropped in June 1940 after roughly eleven years. Start dates are disputed, and the sources are popular history, commentary and a blog. Source: HISTORY (online article, year not shown in the results); Mises Wire (commentary, year not shown in the results); Amusing Planet (online history blog, 2022)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that managers follow market prices within public ownership, so hours and investment respond to demand while a central board sets the rules. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules and the investment, so managers following prices can override hours and leave, and the board's rules can change from above without a vote by the workers affected. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Lange and Taylor, On the Economic Theory of Socialism; Yugoslav workers' self-management

models.best: Inferred from its principle that once the state withers away and classes disappear, distribution follows ability and need, so hours and rest are set by what each person can give and what each requires. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state withers away only after classes disappear, so until then hours and leave can be set by a state that has not yet withered, and the transition may last long with uneven protection for workers. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership of key sectors sits alongside markets and special economic zones, so hours and pay in the zones can follow market conditions while the state keeps key sectors under its direction. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that price reform proceeds gradually under party direction, so hours and leave outside key sectors may follow market pressure and employers' terms, with protection uneven between zones and sectors. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Naughton, The Chinese Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals and balance jobs in complexity, so hours and leave are set by those who do the work and rebalanced across jobs for fairness. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils plan through repeated proposals, so decisions on hours and leave can be slow and time-consuming, and members with less time for deliberation may have less say over their own hours. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into state-controlled corporations, so hours and leave can be set through one bargaining framework for each sector. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state directs industry toward national goals, including war, so hours and leave can be set for output needs, while unions' bargaining is limited inside state-controlled corporations and workers have little voice. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Italian corporative law; Nazi Four-Year Plan

models.best: Inferred from its principle that finance shares profit and risk and that trust underpins contracts, so hours and pay follow shared work and risk, and zakat redistributes wealth to those in need. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that trust underpins contracts, so disputes over hours and leave rest on trust and informal arrangements, with no statutory limit on hours and no formal leave where a contract is weak. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System; Founding of the Mit Ghamr savings bank

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being, so consumption is moderate and work is small-scale, local and non-violent, with hours and rest matched to people's needs rather than to output alone. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that consumption is moderate, so pay gains may be limited, and small local enterprises may give workers no statutory protection on hours or leave. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Buddhist Economics; Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful

models.best: Inferred from its principle that widespread private property and small enterprise give workers a stake in their own work, with a just wage and subsidiarity keeping decisions, including those on hours, with the smallest competent body. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that small enterprise is the norm, so hours and leave depend on each small owner's means, and small firms may lack the scale to offer leave or a set limit on hours, with protection left to the smallest competent body. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum; Belloc, The Servile State

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic activity stays within planetary limits with no growth imperative, so hours can be reduced to share paid work and keep output within those limits. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no growth imperative, so a fall in hours may not be matched by pay that holds up, and a social floor depends on public provision that may not cover every worker's leave or sick pay. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Daly, Steady-State Economics; Raworth, Doughnut Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, so people can take time off paid work, shorten their hours or care for others without losing their basic income. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that income is paid without conditions, so the scheme sets no hours or leave, and employers may cut paid hours and leave because workers can rely on the basic income, with funding from taxes on land and natural resources that may fall short. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Paine, Agrarian Justice; Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government which issues its own currency can fund full employment, so the state can pay for shorter hours and more leave without a borrowing limit, with inflation as the real check. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, so hours and leave schemes funded by currency issue could push prices up if demand outruns output, and workers' real pay and leave may fall. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that communities sharing a resource make and enforce their own rules, so hours and rest in shared work can be set by the community and monitored by its own members. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that rules are designed and enforced locally, so hours and leave may vary unevenly between communities, weaker members may struggle to enforce their rights against stronger ones, and nested institutions may be slow to correct. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons

compromise.summary: A statutory weekly ceiling with averaging only through collective agreement, a legal minimum of paid annual and sick leave, parental leave with months reserved for each parent, and any individual opt-out that is written, revocable on short notice and recorded in hours records.
compromise.details: Keeps: the statutory ceiling with collective averaging (Social market economy; EU Working Time Directive and the UK opt-out), reserved parental months (Nordic social democracy; Sweden's parental insurance and fathers' take-up), and a cap tightened by amendment (Fabian socialism; Britain's Ten Hours Act for textile mills). Blocks: opt-outs that displace the cap (Monetarist neoliberalism), safeguarded by written consent, hours records, no penalty for refusal and seven days' withdrawal notice; unannounced schedule changes (Command socialism), safeguarded by prior consultation; long extra-hours allowances (Developmental state), safeguarded by a 12-hour allowance beyond the 40-hour base; unpaid labour with no leave (Feudalism; Slave economy), safeguarded by statutory paid leave. Test: for five years, measure average weekly hours and the share of workers above 48 hours, whether opt-outs are genuine, and fathers' share of parental days against about 31%. Source: Trades Union Congress report; Population Europe; Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research; Asia News Network; HISTORY; Mount Royal Undergraduate Humanities Review; principles without a case: Bloch, Feudal Society; Williams, Capitalism and Slavery.
